paragraphs: Rabbi Yannai Rabbah: Rabbi was his teacher. Bava Batra 84b: Rabbi Yannai said: Rabbi said. There, 117a as printed (the matching passage is on 113a): Rabbi Yochanan said: Rabbi Yannai said: Rabbi said. But Avodah Zarah 36b has Rabbi Zeira saying: ‘I suffered much over this question with Rabbi Assi; Rabbi Assi with Rabbi Yochanan; Rabbi Yochanan with Rabbi Yannai; Rabbi Yannai with Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram [Natan ben Amram in the Bavli witness]; Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram with Rabbi.’ Thus their order appears: Rabbi Yannai received from Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram, and he from Rabbi. Yevamot 93a gives the sequence: Rav Huna according to Rav—Rashi: he received from his teacher Rav, and likewise all, each above the other from the latter’s teacher; שס״ח [provisionally the new Talmud edition] has each above the other’s generation—Rav according to Rabbi Yannai, Rabbi Yannai according to Rabbi Chiyya, Rabbi Chiyya according to Rabbi, Rabbi according to Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Meir according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov according to Rabbi Akiva. End quotation. Thus Rabbi Yannai according to Rabbi Chiyya, and Rabbi Chiyya according to Rabbi. Rabbi Yannai therefore had Rabbi, Rabbi Chiyya, and Rabbi Yonatan ben Amram as teachers. Responsa Chavvot Yair 94 writes: how can he count three generations from Rav to Rabbi, when Rav served Rabbi? Rabbi Meir too was Rabbi Akiva’s principal student. When Rabbi died, Rabbi Yannai proclaimed: ‘There is no priesthood today’; see his entry. Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Demai, chapter 7: Rabbi Yannai asked Rabbi Chiyya Rabbah, who told him, and so forth: ‘You will one day wield authority over Israel.’ Tosafot, Sukkah 23b, quotes this as ‘He asked Rabbi Chiyya his teacher.’ It seems to me it should read Rabbi Chiyya Rabbah, for that is his usual designation. Yet Yevamot above appears to show Rabbi Chiyya was his teacher, saying Rabbi Yannai according to Rabbi Chiyya. Yevamot 93b, beginning: they showed Rabbi Yannai a broken reed in a dream. He thought the law was not thus; Rabbi Chiyya told him it was another verse, and he had acted well. He sat expounding when a snake came darting: Bereshit Rabbah, chapter 10, Bamidbar Rabbah, chapter 18, Vayikra Rabbah, section 22. Chullin 20a: concerning Rabbi Chiyya’s sons he said, ‘Let the young men receive their answer.’ He was Rabbi Yehudah be-Rabbi Chiyya Rabbah’s father-in-law; see his entry. Rabbi Yannai’s daughters would not be betrothed for less than a tarkav of dinars: Kiddushin 11a. Rabbi Yochanan was his student; see his entry. Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Yannai’s name: Bava Kamma 115a, Bava Metzia 10b, and Yesh Nochalin above. Rabbi Yochanan asked Rabbi Yannai a question before Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak’s bier. He told Rabbi Yochanan: ‘What is the difference between me and you?’ See his entry. Rabbi Yannai said, and so forth; he told Rabbi Yochanan: ‘Had I not lifted the shard for you,’ and so forth. Resh Lakish said: ‘Had not a great man praised you, I would have said,’ and so forth: Makkot 21b and Yevamot 92b, end. Rabbi Yannai said: ‘Thirty elders took a vote: whence do we know that betrothal does not take effect with a woman awaiting levirate marriage?’ Rabbi Yochanan replied: ‘Is it not our Mishnah?’ and so forth. Rabbi Yannai praised him: ‘They pour gold from a purse,’ and so forth; ‘Give to a wise man and he will grow wiser,’ and so forth. Resh Lakish told him: ‘After all this praise, he can explain it according to Rabbi Akiva’: Jerusalem Talmud, Kiddushin 3:5. Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of someone from Rabbi Yannai’s school: Yoma 15a. Beer Sheva, Keritot 5a, writes that one should not read ‘Rabbi Yannai said: Rabbi Yochanan said,’ for Rabbi Yannai was Rabbi Yochanan’s principal teacher. See Zevachim, chapter 2, and what I wrote in the principles.
